questions.stem: An idiolect is:
options: the prestige variety of English expected in formal institutions
the unique variety of language used by one individual
a variety of language shared by a particular social group such as teenagers
a variety of English associated with an ethnic or cultural community
questions.explanation: An idiolect is a person's own way of using language, shaped by everything from where they grew up to their job and interests. A variety shared by a social group is a sociolect.

questions.stem: A sociolect is best defined as:
options: the mixture of two languages that develops when two communities first meet
a variety of language shared by a social group, such as an age group or occupation
the distinctive way that one individual speaks, including their favourite expressions
a variety of language spoken in a particular geographic region of a country
questions.explanation: Sociolects are linked to social variables such as age, occupation, education or interests. A regional variety is a dialect in the geographic sense, and one person's variety is an idiolect.

questions.stem: A speech community is best described as:
options: a group of people who share a language variety and norms for using it
everyone in the world who speaks English as a first or second language
a group of people who have taken the same public-speaking course
the audience that listens to one particular speaker at a public event
questions.explanation: Members of a speech community share not just words but expectations about how to use them. A person belongs to many speech communities at once, such as a family, a school and a sports club.

questions.stem: A person's linguistic repertoire is:
options: the accent they were born with, which stays the same throughout life
the set of grammar rules they were taught at primary school
the full range of languages, varieties and registers they can draw on
the list of words they use most often in their everyday conversation with friends
questions.explanation: A repertoire includes every language, dialect, sociolect and register a speaker commands, from formal Standard English to family slang. The wider the repertoire, the more choices a speaker has to suit a context.

questions.stem: Code switching is best defined as:
options: a gradual change in the meaning of a word over many generations of use
moving between languages or varieties within or across conversations
the unique set of language habits that belongs to one individual speaker
replacing a blunt or taboo word with a milder and more polite alternative
questions.explanation: Code switching is the shift from one language or variety to another, often to signal belonging to the group being addressed. An individual's own habits make up an idiolect, and milder substitutes are euphemisms.

questions.stem: When people choose language to present themselves in a particular way, for example by adopting a group's slang, they are mainly:
options: conveying an identity of their own choosing
having an identity imposed on them by others
losing their idiolect through contact with others
following the overt norms of public institutions
questions.explanation: Identities can be conveyed by the speaker, imposed by others through labels, or negotiated between the two. Choosing a group's slang is the speaker's own act of self-presentation.

questions.stem: Overt prestige is attached to language that:
options: the wider society and its institutions openly regard as correct and educated
a local group values privately, even though wider society may look down on it
is used deliberately to disguise meaning and avoid responsibility
has recently been borrowed from another language through global contact
questions.explanation: Overt prestige belongs to forms, usually those of Standard Australian English, that are publicly recognised as correct and linked with education and status. Prestige within a local group, whatever outsiders think, is covert prestige.

questions.stem: Covert prestige is attached to language that:
options: is publicly recognised by schools, courts and employers as correct and educated
is used only in formal writing that has been edited and proofread
is spoken by the majority of people in a country's capital cities
is valued within a group for signalling belonging, even if non-standard
questions.explanation: Covert prestige is the hidden value of non-standard or local forms that mark someone as one of the group. It works against the overt norms of institutions, which reward Standard English.

questions.stem: A student from a private school drops the g in '-ing' words, says 'yeah nah' and swears more when she is with her local football teammates. This is best explained by:
options: covert prestige, as these features signal belonging within the team
overt prestige, as these features signal her high level of education
a lack of command of Standard English, which she has not yet learned
a speech impairment that affects her pronunciation in noisy places
questions.explanation: With teammates, informal, non-standard features earn acceptance and show she is one of the group. She chooses them for that setting; they say nothing about her command of Standard English, which she presumably uses at school.

questions.stem: In a job interview, a young tradesperson avoids 'youse' and 'reckon', uses full sentences and pronounces '-ing' carefully. He is mainly:
options: using doublespeak to hide his lack of relevant experience
exploiting overt norms to project a competent, educated identity
exploiting covert norms to signal membership of the trades
code switching between two languages to show his heritage
questions.explanation: Shifting towards Standard Australian English in a high-stakes formal setting draws on its overt prestige. Covert norms would be the colloquial forms he chooses to avoid.

questions.stem: In a study of men and women in a British city, many men reported using non-standard pronunciations more often than they actually did. This finding is best explained by:
options: overt prestige, as the men wanted to be seen by the researcher as using the most standard forms available
code switching, as the men were moving between two separate languages during the study
linguistic innovation, as the men had invented new pronunciations during the interviews
covert prestige, as the men valued non-standard forms as markers of toughness and solidarity
questions.explanation: Over-reporting non-standard use suggests the men saw those forms as desirable, which is covert prestige; Peter Trudgill's study in Norwich found this pattern. Women in the same study tended to over-report standard forms, reflecting overt prestige.

questions.stem: In a well-known New York study, shop assistants in an upmarket department store pronounced the r in 'fourth floor' more often than assistants in a cheaper store. This suggests that:
options: staff in the cheaper store had never been taught how to pronounce the sound r correctly
the r in 'fourth floor' carried covert prestige among all the city's speakers
pronunciation in New York varies at random and is not linked to social factors
staff accommodated to the overt prestige of a pronunciation linked to higher status
questions.explanation: William Labov found that use of r in New York rose with the status of the store, showing that a pronunciation with overt prestige was linked to social class and to the identity staff projected. Variation like this is systematic, not random.

questions.stem: Listeners heard the same speaker read a passage twice, once in a Cultivated and once in a Broad accent. They rated the Cultivated reading as more educated but the Broad reading as more friendly. This suggests:
options: accents have no effect on how listeners judge the personality of a speaker
Cultivated features carry overt prestige while Broad features carry solidarity
Broad features carry overt prestige while Cultivated features carry solidarity
listeners judged each reading on the content, which differed between them
questions.explanation: Because the speaker and passage were the same, the different ratings reflect attitudes to the accents themselves. Status judgements point to overt prestige, and warmth judgements to the solidarity associated with covert norms.

questions.stem: A Vietnamese-Australian teenager speaks Vietnamese with her grandmother, then switches to English mid-conversation when her school friends arrive. This is best described as:
options: a false start caused by planning her conversation with her grandmother
code switching to suit the participants and show belonging to each group
morphological over-generalisation caused by learning two languages at once
a loss of fluency in Vietnamese caused by speaking English at school
questions.explanation: Switching languages according to who is present shows skilled use of a bilingual repertoire and signals her connection to both family and friends. It reflects choice, not a loss of fluency.

questions.stem: Two Italian-Australian friends talking in English say 'Nonna made way too much pasta again, mamma mia'. Inserting the Italian words mainly:
options: signals a shared heritage and strengthens their group identity
shows they cannot find the English words they need to express it
creates social distance between the two friends in the conversation
follows the overt norms that institutions expect in formal speech
questions.explanation: Heritage-language words in otherwise English talk mark a shared background and build solidarity between speakers who both understand them. The English equivalents are readily available, so it is a choice rather than a gap.

questions.stem: An Aboriginal teacher uses Aboriginal English with students in the playground and Standard Australian English when writing reports for the principal. This best shows:
options: an inability to use Standard Australian English in spoken settings
the replacement of Aboriginal English by Standard English over time
a breach of overt norms that the school should correct immediately
code switching between varieties according to context and audience
questions.explanation: Moving between Aboriginal English and Standard Australian English according to setting and audience is code switching between varieties, using the full repertoire. It builds connection with students while meeting institutional expectations.

questions.stem: When talking to her new boss, Lauren slows down and adopts some of his more formal vocabulary. In accommodation theory, this is:
options: code switching, moving between two different languages mid-sentence
over-generalisation, applying a grammatical rule where it does not fit
convergence, adjusting speech towards another speaker to reduce distance
divergence, adjusting speech away from another speaker to stress difference
questions.explanation: Convergence moves one's speech closer to an interlocutor's, often to gain approval or build rapport. Divergence emphasises difference, for example by broadening an accent.

questions.stem: A rural farmer, irritated by a condescending city official, deliberately broadens his accent and uses more local slang as the meeting continues. This is best described as:
options: overt prestige, using Standard English forms to sound more educated
divergence, stressing his group identity and distance from the official
convergence, moving his speech closer to the official to gain approval
a loss of control over his speech because of the stress of the meeting
questions.explanation: Moving away from the official's speech asserts the farmer's rural identity and signals resistance, which is divergence. Convergence would move towards the official's more standard speech.

questions.stem: Teenagers often adopt new slang that their parents do not understand, and drop it once adults start using it. This best shows that slang:
options: is the prestige variety expected in formal institutions
never enters general use or appears in dictionaries
marks age-group identity and helps exclude outsiders
is used mainly to show expertise in a professional field
questions.explanation: Slang is a badge of youth identity, so when adults adopt it the word stops marking the group and is often abandoned. Some slang does survive into general use and dictionaries.

questions.stem: An older Australian refers to the radio as 'the wireless' and to a cinema as 'the pictures'. These choices best show:
options: covert prestige, with older speakers using slang to show membership of a youth group
age as a social variable, with older speakers retaining words that have fallen out of use
occupation as a social variable, with technical jargon used only by sound engineers and projectionists
linguistic innovation, with older speakers coining new words to describe technology
questions.explanation: Speakers often keep the words of their youth, so vocabulary varies with age; 'the wireless' is now largely obsolete for radio. These are older words, not new coinages or jargon.

questions.stem: An electrician tells an apprentice to 'check the RCD and run a new circuit off the switchboard'. This use of occupational jargon mainly:
options: communicates precisely and marks both speakers as members of the trade
obscures the meaning so that the apprentice cannot follow the instruction
creates social distance between the electrician and the customer
shows covert prestige by using non-standard grammar from the region
questions.explanation: Between members of a trade, jargon is efficient and confirms shared expertise and identity. The customer is not part of this exchange, and the grammar is standard.

questions.stem: Surfers talk about a 'glassy' morning, 'closeouts' and getting 'barrelled'. These terms best illustrate language variation according to:
options: age
education
geographic region
interests
questions.explanation: Shared interests produce their own vocabularies, and using them marks a person as a member of that community. Surfers of any age, region or education level may use these terms.

questions.stem: A university graduate writing for a journal uses nominalisation, technical terms and long complex sentences. These features mainly reflect variation according to:
options: education, as academic training shapes the language of writing
age, as younger writers prefer shorter, simpler sentences
interests, as surfers and gamers write in the same way
ethnicity, as the writer's heritage language affects syntax
questions.explanation: Academic writing conventions are learned through education, and using them projects an educated, expert identity. Nothing in the description is linked to age or ethnicity.

questions.stem: A man from a working-class background takes public-speaking lessons and changes his vowels to sound more 'polished' before applying for management jobs. This best illustrates language variation according to:
options: age, losing older vocabulary as he grows older and moves on in life
aspiration, adopting overtly prestigious features to suit a desired identity
occupation, using the technical jargon of his current trade in all of his job interviews
interests, using the slang of a hobby to bond with possible employers
questions.explanation: He is changing his speech to fit the identity he wants to have, which is aspiration, drawing on features with overt prestige. The change is deliberate and oriented to the future, not tied to his trade or age.

questions.stem: Linguist Robin Lakoff claimed in the 1970s that women use more hedges, tag questions and intensifiers. Later courtroom research found these features were used by witnesses of both sexes with low status. This suggests that:
options: men never use hedges, tag questions or intensifiers in any context
gender has been proved to have no link to language use at all
such features may relate to power and context, not to gender alone
Lakoff's features are found only in the speech of women in court
questions.explanation: O'Barr and Atkins found the so-called 'women's language' features in the speech of low-status witnesses, male and female, and called them powerless language. That challenges a purely gender-based explanation without proving gender is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Many organisations now use 'chair' or 'chairperson' rather than 'chairman'. This change best shows:
options: a semantic narrowing of the word 'chair' to mean a piece of furniture
changing social attitudes to gender being reflected in language choices
the influence of American English spreading through Australian media
the use of doublespeak to hide who is in charge of an organisation
questions.explanation: As expectations about gender roles shifted, gender-neutral titles were adopted so that the term no longer implies a man holds the role. This is non-discriminatory language driven by social attitudes.

questions.stem: LGBTQIA+ communities have reclaimed 'queer', once used as an insult, as a positive term of self-identification. This is an example of:
options: semantic narrowing, as the word now has fewer meanings
commonisation, as a brand name has become a common noun
a group reclaiming a pejorative term to express its own identity
an outside group imposing an offensive label on a community
questions.explanation: Reclaiming turns a slur into a term of pride used by the group itself, shifting its connotations. The same word used by outsiders as an insult would still be imposing an identity.

questions.stem: A non-binary student asks classmates to use 'they' and 'them' when referring to them. Using these pronouns mainly:
options: creates covert prestige by using non-standard slang from a peer group
reinforces social distance between the student and their classmates
respects the identity the student has chosen to convey through language
breaks a rule of English, as 'they' cannot refer to a single person
questions.explanation: Pronouns signal how people identify, and using requested pronouns respects that identity. Singular 'they' has long been used in English for a person whose gender is unknown or unspecified.

questions.stem: Many autistic adults prefer 'autistic person' to 'person with autism', although some style guides recommend person-first wording. This shows that:
options: person-first language is always the most respectful option for every group and every individual
identity-first language is a form of doublespeak used to hide a diagnosis
style guides have no influence on the language that institutions choose
groups can claim labels that express their identity, sometimes against outside guidance
questions.explanation: Many autistic people see autism as part of who they are, so they choose identity-first wording; this is an identity negotiated by the group itself. The case shows person-first wording is not automatically preferred.

questions.stem: A newspaper describes a group of teenagers as a 'youth gang', although they say they are 'a bunch of mates from school'. The newspaper's label is an example of:
options: an identity imposed on a group by others through language
an identity the group has chosen for itself through slang
code switching between the group's two languages
an archaism preserved in formal newspaper writing
questions.explanation: Labels chosen by outsiders, especially in the media, can impose an identity a group rejects. 'A bunch of mates from school' is how the teenagers present themselves.

questions.stem: A television advertisement shows a tradie with a Broad accent who says 'no worries' and 'she'll be right'. Which statement best describes this representation?
options: It challenges the stereotype that Australian tradespeople speak with a Broad accent
It uses Cultivated features to suggest the tradie is educated and refined
It draws on a familiar stereotype of Australian identity linked to Broad features
It accurately represents the way that every Australian tradesperson speaks at work
questions.explanation: The ad relies on audiences recognising the laconic Broad-accented 'Aussie bloke', a stereotype that can be reassuring but also simplifies real variation. It reinforces rather than challenges the image.

questions.stem: A politician says: 'Hardworking Australians like us are tired of these Canberra insiders telling us what to do.' The contrast between 'us' and 'these Canberra insiders' mainly:
options: follows the overt norms of formal speech to reinforce social distance
uses a euphemism to negotiate a taboo topic in a sensitive manner
constructs an in-group and an out-group to build solidarity with voters
uses jargon to show expertise in the processes of federal parliament
questions.explanation: Pronouns and labels can divide people into 'us' and 'them', aligning the speaker with the audience against an outside group. This is identity construction for persuasion, not technical language.

questions.stem: Online, Mai writes in all lower case, uses ironic emojis and a username built from an in-joke. Offline, at her part-time job, she writes in Standard English. Which statement is most accurate?
options: She constructs different identities for different contexts by drawing on her repertoire
Her online writing shows that she has never properly learned the conventions of Standard English
Her username and emojis prove she has only one fixed identity that never changes
Her online style follows the overt norms that institutions expect in formal writing
questions.explanation: Identity is performed and varies with context: Mai's online choices signal belonging and humour, while her workplace writing projects reliability. Her use of Standard English at work shows she commands it.

questions.stem: Some Australians use hypocoristic nicknames such as 'Davo' or 'Shazza' for friends. This practice mainly:
options: imposes an offensive identity on the person named
follows the overt norms of public institutions
signals friendship and a shared Australian identity
shows formal respect for someone of higher status
questions.explanation: Hypocoristic nicknames express familiarity and are associated with Australian mateship, so they reduce social distance. They would be out of place in formal address to a superior.

questions.stem: A young man avoids words for emotions such as 'heartbroken' among his footy mates and instead says 'pretty rough, mate'. This best shows how:
options: social expectations of a group can shape individual language choices
individuals always choose words without regard to their audience
slang has replaced all words for emotions in Australian English
occupational jargon is used to establish expertise among friends
questions.explanation: Expectations about how members of a group should talk, here ideas about masculinity, can lead speakers to choose understated language. The choice is shaped by audience rather than independent of it.

questions.stem: Two equally qualified applicants apply for a job. The one with a strong migrant accent is not called back, although her written application was excellent. This scenario illustrates:
options: how accents directly show a speaker's intelligence and ability to do a job
how attitudes to accents can lead to discrimination and social disadvantage
how overt prestige rewards speakers who use non-standard varieties of English
how covert prestige helps job applicants who sound different from others
questions.explanation: Judging someone by their accent rather than their ability is linguistic discrimination, and such prejudice can limit access to work. Accents reflect background, not competence.

questions.stem: Some commentators dismiss high rising terminal as a sign that young women lack confidence, yet research finds it is often used by speakers who are confidently holding the floor. This suggests that the criticism:
options: shows that high rising terminal is a non-fluency feature like a false start
proves that intonation carries no meaning in Australian English
reflects attitudes towards the speakers more than the feature's function
is supported by evidence that the feature is used only by young women
questions.explanation: When a feature associated with a social group is criticised regardless of how it works, the judgement usually reflects attitudes to the group. Rising intonation does carry meaning, such as checking that the listener is engaged.

questions.stem: Students whose home variety is Aboriginal English may be marked down in assessments that value only Standard Australian English. This shows how:
options: assessments in schools are unaffected by language attitudes
institutional language expectations can create social disadvantage
Aboriginal English lacks the grammatical rules found in other varieties
covert prestige is rewarded in formal school assessments
questions.explanation: When institutions reward only the standard, speakers of other systematic varieties face a disadvantage that has nothing to do with their ability. Aboriginal English is rule-governed, not deficient.

questions.stem: Some care workers address elderly residents as 'sweetie' and 'love', while some residents find this patronising. This tension shows that:
options: elderly people never value informal language from those caring for them
terms of endearment are a form of jargon used by health professionals
the same language choice can be read as warmth by some and condescension by others
terms of endearment always reinforce social distance between speakers, whatever the context or relationship
questions.explanation: Terms of endearment can build rapport, but from a younger carer they may imply the resident is childlike, threatening their positive face. How a choice is received depends on the participants and their attitudes.

questions.stem: Replacing 'the elderly' with 'older Australians' in government documents mainly aims to:
options: use jargon that only experts in aged care would understand
create a euphemism that hides the topic of ageing altogether
use slang to build solidarity with younger readers
avoid a label that may stereotype people as frail or dependent
questions.explanation: 'The elderly' groups people by a single trait and can carry connotations of frailty, whereas 'older Australians' presents them as members of the community. The topic is still named, so nothing is hidden.

questions.stem: A school captain addressing the assembly says 'we Year 12s' and 'our school', but later, chatting with friends, mocks 'the Year 12 vibe'. This best shows that:
options: inclusive pronouns are used only in informal speech between close friends
speakers present different identities depending on their audience and purpose
the school captain is unable to use formal language in an informal setting
group identity is fixed once it is formed and cannot be negotiated by its individual members
questions.explanation: In the formal role the captain speaks for and with the group; among friends, ironic distance builds a different, more individual identity. Identity is negotiated and shifts with context.
